newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks must be left to market forces -- EPA.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks must be left to market forces -- EPA.

text.p: Prices of shares on the Tokyo stock market must be left to market forces, Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Minister Taro Aso told a news conference on Friday.
"Stocks have fallen... Prices can only be determined by the market," he said, adding, "It's not for the government to intervene."
He said market players appeared to be worried that administrative reforms and deregulation were not taking place fast enough to benefit the Japanese economy.
Aso said that based on past experience, it was easy to understand this view, but added that he believed it would different this time.
He said Japan's economic fundamentals had not changed, but it would be worrying if stocks would not rise.

Japanese stocks took another battering on Friday morning, with the market's key index continuing its slide. At midday the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares was down 428.43 points or 2.37 percent at 17,645.44.

Early in the afternoon, after bouts of selling pressured the Nikkei average down 500 points, short-covering of battered bank shares emerged. The buy-backs by dealers and some foreign investors temporarily shrank the losses, but soon gave way to tidal waves of selling.
"Turnover was quite large today, even without the January option settlements," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities. "Today may have been the selling climax."
Turnover was 809 million shares, nearly double that of Thursday. Losers swamped winners, 1,034 issues to 164, with 852 issues posting new lows.
There were 65 issues which were unchanged.

Friday's fall was the largest single-day drop since the Nikkei average posted a loss of 1,054.72 points -- or 5.6 percent -- on January 23, 1995, when investors dumped Japanese shares on fears that the January 17 Kobe earthquake would take a heavy toll on the economy.

Friday's losses took the Nikkei's cumulative losses for the first week of the new year to 2,057.7 points, or a whopping 10.6 percent, sparking hopes that a rebound might ensue. But many brokers said the market environment was still riddled with too much uncertainty.
"Economic concerns have been hurting the market. On top of that, worries over the financial health of banks are haunting the market, driving it lower," said Sanyo Securities strategist Keiji Arai.

A steep slide in the stock market deals a heavy blow to banks by slashing the paper profits on the shareholdings they own. These unrealised profits are used to tackle the bad loans left over after the collapse of the 1980s asset bubble.
Some brokers added that corporate sales of bank and brokerage shares before the financial year-end book closings at the end of March were accelerating the slide.
"The government is not doing anything to rescue the distressed market and that is adding to the woes," said a trader at a second-tier brokerage.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference that the government was determined to carry out reforms steadily and without fail. He repeated the official view that the economy was gradually recovering and urged firms to have confidence.
Economic Planning Agency Minister Taro Aso told a separate news conference that stock prices can only be determined by the market. "It's not for the government to interfere," he said.
